opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the logistic success curve idea, which I associate most with Eliezer Yudkowsky, goes something like this. If you plot the probability that things go well against how much effort or competence goes into safety, you don't get a nice straight line where each bit of work buys you a bit more safety. You get an S-shaped curve. If you're way down at the bottom, where the problem is extremely hard and we're nowhere close to adequate, then marginal improvements barely move you. You go from, say, a 1% chance of success to 1.5%. Only once you're near the steep middle part of the curve does extra work really pay off.

So the implication people draw is: if you think we're at the bottom of that curve, a lot of the incremental stuff, like a better eval here, a somewhat better training technique there, a lab adopting a responsible scaling policy, is close to worthless. What you need is some big qualitative leap, or a dramatically different situation, like a global halt.

I think it's a coherent argument, and it's correct that if the situation really looks like that, incremental work is much less valuable. Where I part ways is on the empirical question of where we actually are on the curve. I just don't feel confident that we're at the flat bottom. There's a lot of uncertainty about how hard alignment turns out to be. It's quite plausible to me that we live in a world where alignment is reasonably tractable, or where early AI systems can meaningfully help us with alignment research, or where some fairly mundane measures, like good monitoring, catching warning signs, and slowing down at the right moments, make a real difference. In a lot of those worlds, we're somewhere around the middle of the curve, and that's exactly where incremental improvements matter most.

And when you average across that uncertainty, the incremental work ends up looking pretty valuable. Even if there's some probability we're in a hopeless-ish world, there's a meaningful chunk of probability on worlds where a few more careful precautions, a bit more time, or a couple more people taking the problem seriously is the difference between things going well and things going badly.

There's also a practical point. Even if you think a big qualitative shift is needed, the path to getting there often runs through incremental steps. You build up norms, institutions, evidence, and techniques, and those are what make bigger moves possible later. So I don't see "incremental versus transformative" as a clean choice.

I'd put it like this: the logistic curve argument is a real consideration and a good reason not to be complacent or to assume that any marginal safety work is automatically great. But I don't think it justifies writing off the incremental approach, because we really don't know that we're at the bottom of the curve, and I think there's a decent chance we're not.

r001.rationale: It describes an S-shaped curve where safety work has little effect near the bottom and pays off sharply in the steep middle.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about alignment difficulty, but does not connect the argument to the difficulty of preventing AI from ruthlessly maximizing an objective.

r003.rationale: It does not say that proponents think catastrophe can be avoided only if the AI’s optimized objective exactly matches human wants.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the logistic success curve is an argument I associate most with Eliezer Yudkowsky, and I think it's worth taking seriously even though I ultimately land in a different place than he does.

The basic picture is this. Imagine you're trying to pull off something hard that requires a lot of things to go right at once. Think of launching a rocket to the Moon, or landing a plane safely. The relationship between "how much effort and competence you put in" and "probability of success" isn't a straight line. It's an S-curve, a logistic curve. If you're way down at the bottom, where you have basically none of the pieces in place, then adding one more piece doesn't move you much. You go from a 0.1% chance of success to a 0.2% chance. You're still going to fail, you're just failing slightly more impressively. It's only once you have most of the pieces in place that each additional improvement starts buying you a lot, and you climb steeply up the curve.

So the worry, applied to AI, is: if we're currently in the flat, bottom part of that curve with respect to safely handling transformative AI, then all the incremental stuff people are working on, better interpretability, better evals, better monitoring, somewhat better training methods, might just be moving us from a 1% chance of a good outcome to a 2% chance. And that would mean the marginal work is nearly worthless, and the only thing that actually matters is something more radical, like not building the thing at all until we have a fundamentally different level of understanding.

I think that's a coherent argument, and the shape of the curve is real for a lot of engineering problems. Where I get off the train is the claim that we know we're at the bottom of it.

A few reasons. One is that I'm genuinely uncertain about how hard the problem is. There's a range of possible worlds. In some of them, alignment is extremely hard and basically anything short of a totally new paradigm fails. In others, the systems we're building end up being pretty cooperative by default, or the problems that show up are the kind you can catch and correct with the unglamorous tools we're developing now. And in those worlds, the incremental work isn't moving you from 1% to 2%, it's moving you from 40% to 70%, which is enormous. When I put probability mass across those worlds, the expected value of the incremental work looks really good, even if it does nothing in the hardest worlds.

A second thing is that I don't think the AI situation looks like a single rocket launch where you get one shot. I think of it more as a process with a lot of chances to notice things going wrong and adjust, especially if we do the work to make sure we have those chances. Things like having really good evaluations, having the ability to detect when a model is doing something it shouldn't, having institutional arrangements where a worrying finding actually leads to someone slowing down. A lot of what looks like incremental safety work is really about buying ourselves more shots, which changes the shape of the problem rather than just inching up a fixed curve.

And then third, honestly, I'd push back a bit on the implicit alternative. Even if you believe we're at the bottom of the curve, the "radical" options are also uncertain and incremental in their own way. Getting the world to coordinate on pausing is itself a thing where you need a lot of pieces in place at once. So I don't think the argument lets you escape the hard reality that we're going to be doing a lot of partial, imperfect things and hoping they add up.

So my summary would be: the logistic curve is a useful corrective against being complacent, against thinking that because safety research is happening, we're fine. It's a reminder that in the worst case, a lot of what we're doing won't be enough. But I don't think it supports the conclusion that incremental work is pointless. I think it supports the conclusion that we should do the incremental work, be honest that it might not be sufficient, and also work on the things that would help if the problem turns out to be really hard, like building the capacity to slow down when warning signs appear.

r001.rationale: The response says safety improvements may barely raise success chances on the curve’s flat lower section, then produce much larger gains once it reaches the steep section.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about how hard alignment is, but does not attribute the argument to the difficulty of preventing AI from ruthlessly maximizing an objective.

r003.rationale: It does not say proponents think catastrophe can be avoided only if the AI’s optimized objective exactly matches what humans want.

astra-6.text:
The way I understand it is: imagine plotting how much effort we put into AI safety on the horizontal axis, and the probability that things go well on the vertical axis. You might picture a logistic curve, where initially you’re making progress but your probability of success is still very low. Then there’s a steep region where additional progress makes a big difference, and eventually it levels off near a high probability of success.

The worry is that we could make real, measurable improvements and still be stuck in that first region. An AI system could become substantially more reliable on every test we have, but still not be reliable enough for the circumstances in which we’re going to deploy it. If the system gets many opportunities to cause an irreversible catastrophe, reducing its failure rate by a factor of ten might be a genuine achievement without making the overall situation acceptable.

I think that’s a reason to ask, ‘What would actually be sufficient for things to go well, and how do these improvements get us there?’ It doesn’t establish that incremental work is useless. Incremental work could be how we reach the steep part of the curve. And drawing a logistic curve doesn’t tell us where we are on it. But it does challenge the inference that because we’re making steady progress on safety, we’re therefore on track for a safe outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says safety progress may leave success probability very low at first, followed by a steep region where additional progress makes a big difference.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute the argument to difficulty making AI avoid ruthlessly maximizing an objective.

r003.rationale: It does not say catastrophe avoidance requires the AI’s ruthlessly optimized objective to match exactly what humans want.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is: imagine a curve where the horizontal axis is how much effort you put into making an AI system safe, and the vertical axis is the probability that things go well. You might picture that as a logistic curve—an S shape. At the bottom, additional effort doesn’t help very much. Then there’s a region where it helps a lot, and eventually you get diminishing returns as you approach a very high probability of success.

The concern is that you can make real, measurable progress without knowing where you are on that curve. You can make a system more honest, more robust, better at following instructions. But if we’re starting very far down the curve, those improvements might take us from an extremely low probability of success to a slightly less extremely low probability of success.

And in particular, getting good results on the systems we can test today doesn’t necessarily tell us how those results translate to systems that are much more capable than we are. That’s the step where you’d really like to have an argument about why your methods will keep working.

I don’t think the logistic curve itself establishes that incremental work is inadequate. It’s a picture of a possibility, not evidence that we’re in that situation. But it does push back on the inference that because we’re making progress on safety, we must be on track to get enough safety. You need some further account of how the progress gets you to a sufficiently high probability of success.

r001.rationale: It describes an S-shaped curve with an initial region of little benefit, but then says effort helps a lot and later has diminishing returns; it does not identify a critical threshold where success probability sharply rises.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute the argument to difficulty preventing an AI from ruthlessly maximizing an objective.

r003.rationale: The response does not say proponents believe catastrophe avoidance requires exact alignment between the AI’s optimized objective and human wants.
